Dimension. A fundamental invariant of a vector space, defined as the cardinality of any basis—the minimum number of linearly independent vectors needed to generate the entire space. For familiar examples: Euclidean three-space has dimension three, while the space of polynomials of degree at most n has dimension n plus one. Dimension measures the size or degrees of freedom of a vector space.

The dimension of R to the n is n. The dimension of a finite-dimensional vector space is the size of any basis. All bases of a given vector space have the same cardinality—this is the dimension theorem, making dimension well-defined. Vector spaces of different dimensions are never isomorphic. Dimension is the complete topological invariant for finite-dimensional vector spaces.

The basis of a vector space has exactly dim V elements. Any set of more than dim V vectors is linearly dependent. The rank-nullity theorem states that for a linear map from V to W, the dimension of the kernel plus the dimension of the image equals the dimension of V.

Dimension extends to infinite-dimensional spaces, like spaces of functions, where bases may be uncountable. In practical applications, dimension represents degrees of freedom: a rigid body in three-dimensional space has six dimensional freedom—three translational and three rotational. The rank of a matrix is the dimension of its column space, or equivalently, its row space. Rank determines the dimensionality of solutions to linear systems.

Hamel and Schauder bases are two types of bases for infinite-dimensional spaces. The concept of dimension generalizes but loses uniqueness of basis size in these settings.
